title: Stay safe in an earthquake, fire, flood or tsunami
short: Earthquake, tsunami, wildfire, home and high-rise fire, flood, shelter-in-place
intro: What official guides say to do during and right after an earthquake, tsunami warning, wildfire or wildfire smoke, home or high-rise fire, flood, or chemical or radiation emergency, and how to plan an evacuation without a car — and how to get a go-bag and family plan ready beforehand. Many readings are from US agencies; local rules, emergency numbers and services differ.

choices.label: The ground is shaking right now
choices.hint: Earthquake — indoors, in bed, outside or driving

read.label: Drop, Cover and Hold On in an earthquake (FEMA)
read.note: 2024 sheet from FEMA (the US federal emergency agency): what to do indoors, in bed, in a vehicle or high-rise, and going inland after shaking if tsunamis are possible.

read.label: Why not to run outside or stand in a doorway (CERT)
read.note: CERT (US community volunteer responder training) manual: during shaking in a car, in bed, outdoors or near the coast, plus first steps if you are trapped.

read.label: What to do during an earthquake (FEMA P-530)
read.note: Detailed survival guidance from FEMA's home earthquake guide, including what to do with no table nearby.

read.label: First checks after an earthquake (CERT)
read.note: Check yourself, then others; put out small fires; clean up spills; inspect for damage; expect aftershocks; tune to emergency broadcasts.

read.label: What NOT to do after an earthquake
read.note: No candles or flames until you know there's no gas leak, don't turn gas back on yourself, unplug appliances, text rather than call.

read.label: Home safety checklist: gas and fuel tanks
read.note: Start of FEMA's room-by-room post-earthquake checklist; later pages cover electrical, water, chimneys and solar panels.

choices.label: Tsunami warning, or a strong quake at the coast
choices.hint: Near the beach, harbour or low ground by the ocean

read.label: Tsunami safety: natural vs official warnings (NWS)
read.note: US National Weather Service (NWS): go to high ground or inland right away after a strong quake at the coast; plan to evacuate on foot; a cancelled warning doesn't mean safe.

read.label: Tsunami watch, advisory and warning explained
read.note: CERT: what each US alert level means and that the first wave may arrive before a warning.

read.label: During and after a tsunami
read.note: Higher ground or upper floors of a tall sturdy building, boats, and why to wait for officials — the next wave can be larger.

read.label: How to stay safe when a tsunami threatens (FEMA)
read.note: Prepare, survive, be safe: shelters 100 feet (30 m) up or a mile (1.6 km) inland, evacuation route signs, electrocution risk in floodwater.

choices.label: A wildfire is near — evacuate or trapped
choices.hint: Evacuation order, fire approaching, trapped at home or in a car

read.label: Before you evacuate from a wildfire (Ready.gov)
read.note: Ready.gov (the US government preparedness site): the Five Ps to take, and steps that help firefighters if there's time: lights on, windows closed, garage opener disconnected.

read.label: Driving away, or trapped at home or in a car
read.note: Driving through smoke, and last-resort actions if trapped in your home, a vehicle or outdoors.

read.label: How to stay safe when a wildfire threatens (FEMA)
read.note: Leave immediately when told, call the emergency number if trapped, use N95 masks, and avoid hot ash and embers after.

choices.label: Wildfire smoke is making the air bad
choices.hint: Smoky air, not ordered to evacuate

read.label: Protecting yourself from smoke (Ready.gov)
read.note: N95 masks, a closed-off room with a portable air cleaner, high-efficiency filters in the heating or air-conditioning system set to recirculate, and extra caution for lung conditions.

read.label: N95 respirators for wildfire smoke (FEMA)
read.note: Gather N95 masks ahead of time and use them to keep particles out of the air you breathe.

choices.label: Fire in the home
choices.hint: Smoke alarm going off, fire or smoke inside

read.label: Red Cross: get out and stay out
read.note: Crawl low, check door handles with the back of your hand, signal from a window if trapped, never go back in.

read.label: If trapped by smoke, and after a fire (CERT)
read.note: Staying low near a window and signalling the fire department; electrical dangers when returning after a fire.

read.label: Home fire escape plans (US Fire Administration)
read.note: You may have less than 2 minutes to escape; two ways out of every room, a meeting place, and high-rise advice.

choices.label: Fire in an apartment or high-rise building
choices.hint: Alarm in the building, smoke in the hallway, stairs or elevator

read.label: Leaving a high-rise apartment in a fire (US Fire Administration)
read.note: US Fire Administration (USFA) page: high-rise fires are especially dangerous; leave, close the door behind you, pull the alarm, take the stairs, not the elevator unless firefighters direct it.

read.label: Red Cross: if you can't reach the exit stairs
read.note: Red Cross sheet (2014): if trapped, call the emergency number, close doors, hang a white sheet outside the window; practise reaching the fire stairs or a safe place in your unit.

read.label: No elevators, hot doors, and being trapped in a room (CERT)
read.note: CERT 2019 annex: never using an elevator to escape, checking a door for heat and smoke, and sealing gaps with wet cloth if all exits are blocked.

read.label: Know two ways out of your building
read.note: Ready.gov page (2026): in a high-rise, knowing the closest exit and a second way out, not using elevators, and keeping right on stairwells so emergency workers can come up.

read.label: How to stay safe when a flood threatens (FEMA)
read.note: Evacuate when told, don't walk or drive through floodwater, avoid closed attics, and electrical and generator hazards after.

read.label: Turn Around, Don't Drown and flood steps
read.note: FEMA's Are You Ready? guide: how little moving water can sweep you or a car away, going to higher levels, and after-flood electrocution risks.

choices.label: I may need to evacuate and have no car
choices.hint: Bus, train, accessible transport (paratransit), a ride from neighbours or family

read.label: Planning evacuation without a car (Are You Ready?)
read.note: FEMA Are You Ready? guide (2020): planning transport with family, friends or local government if you have no car, and checking on neighbours who may need a ride.

read.label: Public and accessible transport in an evacuation
read.note: FEMA wildfire guide (written 2014, reposted 2020): arranging shared rides and asking local emergency management how evacuation by public or accessible transport works, including staging areas.

read.label: Meeting places and backup ways to get out
read.note: FEMA Are You Ready? (2020): meeting places in several directions that everyone can reach, and learning alternate routes and backup ways to travel out of your area.

read.label: Commuter plan: write down routes, buses and trains
read.note: Ready.gov fill-in form (2013): normal and alternative routes between work and home, public transport lines and stops, and taxi and local bus numbers.

choices.label: Chemical or radiation emergency — told to shelter
choices.hint: Shelter-in-place order, chemical release, nuclear incident

read.label: Sealing a room for a chemical release (CERT)
read.note: Shutting off ventilation, plastic sheeting and duct tape, how long you'd typically stay, and ventilating afterwards.

read.label: Red Cross: chemical threat — what to do
read.note: Shelter in place by closing windows and fans, wet cloths if no tape, and calling a poison centre or the emergency number.

read.label: Nuclear explosion: get inside, stay inside (FEMA)
read.note: Best shelter locations, at least 10 minutes to find shelter, removing and washing off fallout, and safe food and water.

read.label: Nuclear power plant emergency (CERT)
read.note: Follow local instructions, sheltering vs evacuating, closing air intakes, and showering and bagging clothes after exposure.

limits.text: Do NOT get in a doorway during an earthquake — it doesn't protect from falling objects — and do not run outside.
If there are major cracks in the chimney or foundation, or the home or its utilities have shifted, get everyone out.
If you turned the gas off, do not turn it on again yourself; let the gas company inspect and restore it.
Do not use matches, lighters, candles, camp stoves or electrical equipment until you are sure there are no gas leaks.
If crawlspace walls have slid or are visibly leaning, turn off gas at the meter and do not move back in until the home has been checked for safety.
Damaged or shifted rooftop solar panels are a falling or fire hazard; switch off the solar feed if possible and contact a qualified professional.
In a tsunami area, after a strong quake or a natural warning go to high ground or inland at once — do not wait for an official warning.
A tsunami is a series of waves that may continue for hours; the next wave may be larger. Return only when officials say it is safe.
If authorities tell you to evacuate for a wildfire, leave immediately; if trapped, call the emergency number, but help could be delayed or impossible.
Authorities will never advise you to stay and fight an approaching wildfire.
Once out of a burning home, stay out; never go back inside for possessions, pets or people.
Do not walk, swim or drive through floodwater; just a foot (30 cm) of moving water can sweep a vehicle away. Do not climb into a closed attic.
Underground or downed power lines can electrically charge water; do not touch electrical equipment if it is wet or you are standing in water.
Young children and older adults should not use fire extinguishers; ask the fire department for training.
Outdoor areas, vehicles and mobile homes do NOT provide adequate shelter from nuclear fallout.
In a high-rise fire, use the stairs; do not use the elevator unless the fire department tells you to.
Never open a door that feels hot. If smoke, heat or flames block every exit, stay in the room with the door closed and call the fire department to say where you are.

prepare.label: Create a family disaster plan (CERT)
prepare.note: Two meeting places, an out-of-area contact, wallet cards, shutting off utilities, alarms, and meeting neighbours.

prepare.label: Red Cross: make a plan
prepare.note: Two exits from every room, two meeting places, an out-of-area contact, and texting because phone lines get overwhelmed.

prepare.label: Emergency supply kit checklist (FEMA, 2024)
prepare.note: Basic kit items — water, food, radio with weather alerts, flashlight, whistle, masks, plastic sheeting, utility wrench — and extras on the reverse.

prepare.label: The Five Ps of evacuation and a go-bag
prepare.note: People, Prescriptions, Papers, Personal needs, Priceless items, and storing important documents safely.

prepare.label: Earthquake-proof your home
prepare.note: CERT: practise Drop, Cover and Hold On, secure furniture and water heaters, keep shoes and a flashlight by the bed, and use licensed professionals for flexible gas lines.

prepare.label: Plan your tsunami evacuation route
prepare.note: Know your inundation zone and street elevation, natural warning signs, and plan routes you can follow at night.

prepare.label: Prepare home and family for wildfires (Ready.gov)
prepare.note: Alerts, evacuation zones, a 30-foot (9 m) fire-resistant zone, a clean-air room, N95 masks and backup charging.

prepare.label: Liquefaction and tsunami: why soil matters
prepare.note: FEMA P-530 explains how loose wet soil can turn to quicksand in a quake, plus how tsunamis form. Relevant for sandy coastal areas.

learn.label: Hazard information sheets (FEMA, 2024)
learn.note: Full set of two-page sheets for every major hazard, from earthquake and tsunami to power outage and nuclear explosion.

learn.label: Are You Ready? guide (FEMA, 2020)
learn.note: FEMA's in-depth citizen preparedness guide: hazard-by-hazard actions, making a plan, supplies and recovery.

learn.label: Earthquake Safety at Home (FEMA P-530, 2020)
learn.note: Prepare, protect, survive, respond and recover — including retrofit projects and a full post-quake home checklist.

learn.label: CERT Hazard Annexes (2019)
learn.note: Detailed before/during/after guidance and myths vs facts for earthquake, fire, flood, tsunami, nuclear and more.

learn.label: CERT Basic Training Participant Manual (2019)
learn.note: Neighbourhood volunteer training: preparedness, fire safety and utilities, first aid, light search and rescue, terrorism.

learn.label: Red Cross Be Prepared guide
learn.note: Red Cross regional guide covering kits, plans and hazards such as earthquake, tsunami and wildfire.

learn.label: Building homes in wildfire zones (FEMA P-754)
learn.note: FEMA guide on how homes ignite in wildfires and construction details that resist embers and flames.

learn.label: Tsunami warning fact sheet (NOAA)
learn.note: How NOAA (the US weather and oceans agency) detects tsunamis and issues warnings.

learn.label: Protective Action Guides for radiological incidents (EPA)
learn.note: Planning manual from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for officials on when to shelter or evacuate after radiation releases. Technical; written for emergency planners.

learn.label: Nuclear War Survival Skills (Kearny)
learn.note: Classic civil-defence book from the 1980s on fallout shelters and expedient protection. Historical — prefer current official guidance.
